html:
A reality check dressed as a chuckle

The world feels like it’s on fire.

Millions are in distress. Those who were already walking the tightrope of survival are now terrified, not of ambition or failure, but of something far more primal. In India, families are fighting for something as basic as cooking gas. Education, mental health, a child’s future all get quietly shelved when the only question left is: will we eat today?

People I know — people from the same lower-middle-class neighbourhoods, the same IT corridors, the same generation that believed the industry was our ladder out are now wondering if the rungs will hold. Not just for themselves For their children. The unspoken question in their eyes: Will my child have a better life than mine?

That’s not a small thing to carry.

And then, into this heaviness, WordPress sent me a prompt.

“What makes you laugh, Sakti?”

I sat with it. And somewhere between the exhaustion and the noise, something cracked open not grief, not rage. A laugh. A real one.

Here’s what makes me laugh.

That we took things for granted. That we assumed what exists today will exist tomorrow. That we believed the skills of yesterday are the currency of tomorrow. That we imagined life moves in a straight line —upward, orderly, predictable.

That makes me laugh.

It makes me laugh that I once thought what my parents knew was outdated. And now I catch myself assuming my children know less than me. As if wisdom flows in one direction. As if time doesn’t have its own sense of humour.

It makes me laugh that I thought being articulate, writing well, speaking in full sentences, dropping the right references, made me thoughtful. That performing intelligence is the same as possessing it.

It makes me laugh that the friends I neglected, the ones I was too busy or too proud to call, were the ones who showed up when it mattered. Quietly. Without announcement.

It makes me laugh that I once confused flattery for friendship. That people who said only good things about me, who never disagreed or pushed back, felt like my tribe. When really, they were just mirrors — telling me what I wanted to see.

And here’s the deepest laugh of all.

My belief that I know and my ignorance of the fact that I don’t.

This isn’t a tired Sunday night thought spiral. This isn’t performative humility dressed up in blog-post language. This is the oldest realisation in the book, wearing new clothes, catching me off guard again.

The Upanishads have a name for it. Avidya — the ignorance that doesn’t announce itself. It doesn’t feel like confusion. It feels like certainty. That’s what makes it so quietly dangerous. And, when you finally see it, so genuinely funny.

The world is heavy right now. The macro is grim. The anxiety is real.

But maybe laughter, not the escaping kind, the seeing kind, is its own form of clarity.

Maybe looking at ourselves without the armour of our assumptions, our credentials, our curated self-image, is not defeat. Maybe it’s the beginning of something more honest.

So yes. I’m laughing.

Not because things are fine. But because I finally see a few things more clearly than I did yesterday.

And that, I think, is worth something.

What about you — what’s a belief you held tightly that life gently (or not so gently) corrected?
